lesson.title: Off the Line, Not Off the Chart: Outliers in Regression
lesson.summary: A regression outlier is a point with an unusually large residual, a y-value that departs sharply from the model's prediction, which is a different thing from an unusual x-value or an outlier in a single variable.
lesson.body:
The word "outlier" gets used loosely, but in regression it has a specific meaning distinct from what it means for a single list of numbers. A regression outlier is a point whose residual is unusually large in absolute value, meaning its actual y-value is far from what the regression line predicts for its x-value, even if that x-value itself looks completely ordinary. This is a different idea from an outlier in one variable alone (a value far from the rest of a list) and a different idea from leverage (an unusual x-value); a regression outlier is about the vertical distance between a point and the line, not its horizontal position. A point can even be perfectly ordinary in both its x-value and its y-value considered separately, and still count as a regression outlier, if that particular combination of x and y falls far from the trend the rest of the data follows.

Consider a variation on the study-hours data set. Suppose a sixth student studied 3 hours, squarely in the middle of the observed range of 1 to 5, but scored only 20 on the exam. Using the original fitted line, y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1x, the predicted score at x = 3 is y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1(3) = 71.6. The residual for this student is 20 - 71.6 = -51.6, an enormous miss compared to the residuals of -0.4 to 1.5 seen among the other five students. This is a textbook regression outlier: an ordinary, centrally located x-value paired with a wildly unexpected y-value. On a scatterplot, this point would sit far below the cluster formed by the other five points, a gap that would be obvious to the eye even without calculating the residual.

Compare this to the influential point from earlier, the student who studied 20 hours and scored 40. That point had both an extreme x-value (high leverage) and a residual that broke the pattern, which is exactly why it was influential enough to flip the slope. The new x = 3, y = 20 point, by contrast, has low leverage, because x = 3 sits close to the mean of x, at about the center of the data's pull. Because of its low leverage, adding this point would inflate the sum of squared residuals substantially and lower r-squared, but it would not swing the slope nearly as violently, since a centrally located point simply does not have the same lever arm to rotate the line. It would, however, still be worth flagging and investigating, since a residual of -51.6 out of a total score range of roughly 55 to 88 is far too large to dismiss as ordinary scatter.

This distinction matters because it shows that "outlier" and "influential" are not synonyms in regression, even though they overlap in everyday language. A point can be a dramatic outlier in its residual and still leave the line almost exactly where it was, if that point sits near the center of x. Conversely, a point can look unremarkable in its residual and still be influential, if its extreme x-value gives it enough leverage to pull the line even a modest amount. Checking both the size of a point's residual and its position along the x-axis, rather than relying on a single label like "outlier," is what a careful regression analysis requires, and it is exactly the combination of ideas, residuals from calculating residuals and leverage from position along x, that the concept of an influential point was built to capture.
